_note: Ranking Languages by How Many Accent Marks They Have. Count = lowercase letters with diacritics in the official alphabet (precomposed; ligatures like œ/æ and separate letters like ß/þ/ð not counted). Vietnamese: 12 vowels x 5 tone marks + ă â ê ô ơ ư đ = 67. Ties (9) broken by how many different kinds of marks: Polish and Lithuanian use 4, Hungarian 3. Each word is a real Lingua Libre recording (viewer idea from the comments).
title: Ranking Languages by How Many Accent Marks They Have
subtitle: LETTERS WITH ACCENT MARKS IN THE ALPHABET
outro: Which accent mark do you love (or hate)?

items.name: Vietnamese
cards: 67 accented letters: 12 vowels, each with up to five tone marks, plus ă, â, ê, ô, ơ, ư and đ.
Some letters stack two marks: the ệ in 'Việt' has a hat for the vowel and a dot below for the tone.

items.name: Slovak
cards: Slovak has 17, more than Czech: it adds ä, ĺ, ľ, ô and ŕ.
Long ĺ and ŕ are consonants that work as vowels: 'vŕba' means willow.

items.name: Czech
cards: Czech has 15, including ř, a sound that almost no other language has.
The little ring in ů shows where an o used to be: 'kůň' (horse) was once 'kóň'.

items.name: French
cards: French has 14. The letter ù appears in just one word: 'où', where.
The circumflex often marks a lost s: 'forêt' was 'forest' and 'hôpital' was 'hospital'.

items.name: Portuguese
cards: The tilde makes vowels nasal: 'pão' is bread and 'corações' is hearts.
A 1990 spelling agreement between Portuguese-speaking countries removed some accents, like the ü.

items.name: Latvian
cards: A line on top makes a vowel long: ā, ē, ī, ū.
ķ, ļ and ņ get a little comma underneath for a soft sound, and ģ gets one on top.

items.name: Polish
cards: Nine letters: ą ć ę ł ń ó ś ź ż, with four different kinds of marks. And ł sounds like an English w.
'Zażółć gęślą jaźń' (paint the soul yellow with a fiddle) uses all nine in three words.

items.name: Lithuanian
cards: Also nine, also four kinds of marks: ą ę į ų have a little tail called an ogonek, and ė is a closed e.
Lithuanian took č, š and ž from Czech spelling in the 1800s.

items.name: Hungarian
cards: Hungarian is famous for the double acute: ő and ű are long versions of ö and ü.
'Árvíztűrő tükörfúrógép' (flood-proof mirror drill) contains all nine accented letters.

items.name: Spanish
cards: The ñ started as a little n written over another n to save space: 'anno' became 'año'.
Accents change meaning: 'papa' is potato, 'papá' is dad.
